job.style: a diary entry or letter by a student

passage: Dear Diary, today my father explained why we must be careful with money. He showed me two loan offers for a new bike. One bank uses a flat rate of 8%, while the other uses a reducing-balance rate of 8%. He warned that the flat rate is actually much more expensive because you pay interest on the full amount even as you pay it back. He also checked a credit card statement, noting that the interest-free period only applies if you pay the full bill, not just a part of it. We then calculated interest for a six-month loan. Since the formula uses time in years, we had to use 0.5 years, not 6, to get the correct amount. Finally, he explained that while a 10-year loan has a smaller monthly EMI, you end up paying much more in total interest than with a 2-year loan. I realized that borrowing is not just about the interest rate or the monthly payment; it is about the total cost over time. I must always check the fine print before agreeing to any loan or using a credit card.

items.evidence: He warned that the flat rate is actually much more expensive because you pay interest on the full amount even as you pay it back.
items.q: Both bike loans charge 8%. Why does the father say the flat-rate loan is much more expensive?
options: Its interest is charged on the whole loan till the end
Its 8% rate goes up a little every year
Its interest is charged on a balance that keeps shrinking
Its 8% is charged per month, not per year
items.explain: With a flat rate you keep paying interest on the full amount, even after you have paid part of it back.

wrong.why: thinks the rate itself keeps increasing
mixes up the flat rate with the reducing-balance rate
thinks a rate means per month unless stated

items.evidence: He also checked a credit card statement, noting that the interest-free period only applies if you pay the full bill, not just a part of it.
items.q: Meena's credit card bill is ₹5,000. She pays ₹3,000 within the interest-free period. What happens?
options: She loses the interest-free benefit, as she paid only part
She pays no interest, as she paid within the free period
She pays no interest, as she paid more than half
She pays interest only on the ₹3,000 she already paid
items.explain: The interest-free period applies only if the full bill is paid. Meena paid only part, so she loses it.

wrong.why: thinks a part payment still gets the interest-free period
over-generalises: thinks paying most of the bill is enough
mixes up the amount paid with the amount still owed

items.evidence: Since the formula uses time in years, we had to use 0.5 years, not 6, to get the correct amount.
items.q: Priya finds simple interest on a six-month loan using SI = PRT/100. What should she put for T?
options: T = 0.5, because six months is half a year
T = 6, because the loan lasts six months
T = 1, because time does not change the interest
T = 12, because a year has twelve months
items.explain: The formula uses time in years, and six months is half a year, so T = 0.5.

wrong.why: puts the number of months straight into the formula
thinks interest does not depend on time
confuses months in a year with the loan's time

items.evidence: Finally, he explained that while a 10-year loan has a smaller monthly EMI, you end up paying much more in total interest than with a 2-year loan.
items.q: Ravi chooses a 10-year bike loan over a 2-year one because its EMI is smaller. What will happen?
options: He will pay far more interest over the whole loan
He will pay less in total, as each EMI is smaller
He will pay the same interest, as time does not matter
He will pay just the loan amount split into more months
items.explain: A 10-year loan has a smaller EMI, but you pay much more total interest than with a 2-year loan.

wrong.why: thinks smaller EMIs mean a smaller total cost
thinks interest does not depend on time
thinks an EMI is just the loan divided by the months
